briefOverview: Paul concludes Romans with commendations and greetings, warns against divisive teachers, and closes with a doxology exalting God for revealing the gospel to all nations.
summary: Paul commends Phebe, a servant of the church in Cenchrea, urging the Romans to receive and assist her. He sends extensive greetings to many co-workers and households, highlighting the sacrificial help of Priscilla and Aquila, the early faith of Andronicus and Junia, and the labors of numerous women and men in the Lord. He instructs the believers to greet one another with a holy kiss and conveys greetings from the churches of Christ. Paul warns them to watch out for those who cause divisions contrary to the teaching they learned and to avoid such people, noting their deceptive speech. He encourages the Romans for their obedience, advising them to be wise concerning good and innocent concerning evil, and promises that the God of peace will soon crush Satan under their feet. Final greetings come from Timothy, Paul’s kinsmen, Tertius the scribe, Gaius the host, Erastus the city official, and Quartus. Paul ends with a doxology praising God who strengthens believers through the proclaimed gospel, the once-hidden but now revealed mystery, made known to all nations to bring about the obedience of faith.
externalContext: Cenchrea was the eastern port of Corinth, suggesting the letter was written from the Corinth area during Paul’s third missionary journey (mid–50s CE). The mention of Tertius reflects the common ancient practice of using an amanuensis (scribe) to write letters. Early Christian communities met in house churches, often hosted by patrons or well-resourced believers (e.g., Priscilla and Aquila). The “holy kiss” was a customary greeting in the ancient Mediterranean adapted as a sign of Christian fellowship. Names listed include slaves, freedpersons, Jews, and Gentiles, illustrating the diverse social makeup of Roman house churches.
externalReferences: Priscilla and Aquila are known co-workers who hosted a church and worked with Paul (Acts 18:2–3; 1 Corinthians 16:19). Erastus appears in Acts 19:22 and 2 Timothy 4:20, possibly the same city official mentioned here. The doxology’s language of the “obedience of faith” echoes Romans 1:5, and its “mystery now revealed” parallels Ephesians 3:3–6 and Colossians 1:26–27. The promise that God will “bruise” or crush Satan under believers’ feet resonates with Genesis 3:15.
practicalQuestions: How can I tangibly support and commend faithful servants and messengers in the church today?
Where might smooth-sounding teaching be promoting division, and how can I wisely avoid it while preserving unity?
What does it look like to be “wise about what is good and simple concerning evil” in my media, relationships, and habits?
How can my home or resources serve as a base for ministry and community, as with early house churches?
How might I practice culturally appropriate signs of warm, holy fellowship that build genuine unity?
uncertainAreas: The phrase “of note among the apostles” regarding Andronicus and Junia is debated (whether Junia is female and whether they are counted as apostles or esteemed by the apostles). “Firstfruits of Achaia” for Epaenetus may reflect a textual variant with “Asia” in some manuscripts. The timing and manner of “God… shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly” is not specified. The identification of Rufus with the Rufus in Mark 15:21 is possible but not certain.
